question: Where must an operator set out the principles and methods of its loading and mass and balance system?

options.text: On the load sheet of each individual flight
In the Operations Manual
In the certificate of airworthiness
In the aeroplane's technical log only

explanation: The operator's loading and mass and balance system is described in the Operations Manual and must cover every type of operation it intends to fly. The load sheet applies that system to one flight; it does not define it.

question: Which standard masses may an operator use for crew members when it builds up the dry operating mass?

options.text: 75 kg per flight crew member and 85 kg per cabin crew member
84 kg for every crew member, flight deck or cabin
85 kg per flight crew member and 75 kg per cabin crew member
88 kg per flight crew member and 70 kg per cabin crew member

explanation: The standard crew masses are 85 kg for flight crew and 75 kg for cabin crew, both including hand baggage. The 88/70 kg pair is the male/female passenger mass, which students often confuse with the crew figures.

question: Besides the standard crew masses, which other crew mass values may an operator use for the dry operating mass?

options.text: Only the masses printed in the aeroplane flight manual
Estimated masses declared verbally by each crew member
The passenger all-adult standard mass for every crew member
Actual masses including crew baggage, or other approved standard masses

explanation: The operator may use actual masses (including any crew baggage), the standard 85/75 kg values, or other standard masses acceptable to the authority. Verbal statements are a passenger method for small aeroplanes, not a crew method.

question: Crew carry more baggage than the dry operating mass allows for. What must the operator do?

options.text: Correct the DOM and use the baggage position for the CG
Nothing, because crew baggage is always inside the standard crew mass
Reduce the trip fuel by the mass of the extra baggage
Treat the extra baggage as traffic load and leave the CG unchanged

explanation: Additional crew baggage changes both the dry operating mass and the CG, so the DOM must be corrected and the position of that baggage used when the CG is worked out. Ignoring its position would give a wrong CG even if the mass were right.

question: In general, how may an operator determine the mass of passengers and checked baggage?

options.text: Only by using the standard mass tables
By asking each passenger for a verbal statement
By actual weighing or by using the standard mass tables
Only by weighing every passenger and every bag

explanation: The rule allows either the actual weighed mass of each person and bag or the standard mass values from the tables. Verbal statements are allowed only on aeroplanes with fewer than 10 passenger seats.

question: Below what number of passenger seats may passenger mass be found from a verbal statement plus a fixed allowance?

options.text: Fewer than 6 seats
Fewer than 10 seats
Fewer than 20 seats
Fewer than 30 seats

explanation: On aeroplanes with fewer than 10 passenger seats, each passenger's stated mass may be used with a predetermined constant added for hand baggage and clothing. The 20- and 30-seat thresholds belong to the standard mass tables, not to verbal statements.

question: When passenger mass comes from a verbal statement, what is added to each stated mass?

options.text: A fixed constant for hand baggage and clothing
The standard mass of one checked bag for that route
Nothing; the stated mass is used as given
A 6 kg allowance for a child under two years

explanation: A verbal statement covers only the person, so a fixed constant is added to account for hand baggage and clothing. The procedure for this, and for choosing between actual and standard masses, must be in the Operations Manual.

question: When passengers are weighed rather than given standard masses, what must the weighing include and when must it be done?

options.text: Hand baggage only, at any time on the day of departure
Personal belongings, at the passenger's home airport
Body mass only, at check-in on the day before
Belongings and hand baggage, just before boarding

explanation: Weighed masses must include personal belongings and hand baggage, and the weighing must take place immediately before boarding at a location close to the aeroplane. That way the mass cannot change before the passenger boards.

question: What do the standard passenger masses already include?

options.text: Clothing only; hand baggage is added at 6 kg per passenger
Hand baggage only; infants are always added separately
Hand baggage and any infant under two carried on an adult's seat
Checked baggage and the passenger's hand baggage

explanation: The standard passenger masses include hand baggage and the mass of an infant under two years carried by an adult on one seat. Checked baggage has its own standard values.

question: An infant under two years occupies a separate passenger seat. How is it counted for standard masses?

options.text: As included in the accompanying adult's mass
As a child
As zero mass, because infants are exempt
As an adult female

explanation: Only an infant sharing an adult's seat is inside the adult's standard mass. An infant in its own seat counts as a child, which is 35 kg in the tables.

question: With 20 or more passenger seats, which standard masses apply?

options.text: The separate male and female masses
The 1–5 seat masses from the small aeroplane table
Actual weighed masses only
The all-adult mass only

explanation: From 20 seats upward the male and female standard masses apply. The all-adult value is an alternative only from 30 seats upward.

question: From how many passenger seats may the "all adult" standard mass be used instead of the male and female values?

options.text: 40 or more
20 or more
10 or more
30 or more

explanation: The all-adult mass is an alternative to the male/female values only on aeroplanes with 30 or more passenger seats. Between 20 and 29 seats the male/female values must be used.

question: For standard masses, what is a holiday charter?

options.text: Any flight that departs during a school holiday period
Any charter flight carrying fewer than 30 passengers
A scheduled flight that carries mainly tourists
A charter flight solely part of a holiday travel package

explanation: A holiday charter is a charter flight intended solely as an element of a holiday travel package. Its lower standard masses apply only if non-revenue carriage of certain passengers uses no more than 5% of the installed seats.

question: The holiday charter masses apply only if non-revenue passengers of certain categories occupy no more than what share of the installed seats?
explanation: The holiday charter values may be used provided that not more than 5% of the installed passenger seats are used for non-revenue carriage of certain categories of passengers. Above that, the normal values apply.

question: On a flight that is not a holiday charter, with 20 or more seats, what are the standard male and female passenger masses?

options.text: Male 92 kg, female 74 kg
Male 83 kg, female 69 kg
Male 88 kg, female 70 kg
Male 84 kg, female 70 kg

explanation: For all flights except holiday charters the values are 88 kg male and 70 kg female. 83/69 kg are the holiday charter values and 92/74 kg belong to aeroplanes with 10–19 seats.

question: What is the "all adult" standard passenger mass on a normal (non-holiday) flight with 30 or more seats?

options.text: 84 kg
88 kg
76 kg
79 kg

explanation: The all-adult mass is 84 kg on all flights except holiday charters, where it is 76 kg. It blends male and female masses in a fixed ratio.

question: What are the holiday charter standard masses for male, female and all-adult passengers?

options.text: 88, 70 and 84 kg
86, 69 and 76 kg
83, 70 and 84 kg
83, 69 and 76 kg

explanation: Holiday charters use 83 kg male, 69 kg female and 76 kg all-adult. The normal values are 88, 70 and 84 kg.

question: What standard mass is used for a child (2 years or older) on any aeroplane?

options.text: 40 kg
25 kg
35 kg
30 kg

explanation: Children are 35 kg in every column of both standard mass tables, whatever the number of seats or type of flight.

question: On an aeroplane with 1 to 5 passenger seats, what are the standard male and female masses?

options.text: Male 88 kg, female 70 kg
Male 104 kg, female 86 kg
Male 92 kg, female 74 kg
Male 96 kg, female 78 kg

explanation: Smaller aeroplanes use heavier standard masses because a few unusually heavy passengers matter more. With 1–5 seats the values are 104 kg male and 86 kg female.

question: On an aeroplane with 6 to 9 passenger seats, what are the standard male and female masses?

options.text: Male 96 kg, female 78 kg
Male 92 kg, female 74 kg
Male 96 kg, female 74 kg
Male 104 kg, female 86 kg

explanation: The 6–9 seat values are 96 kg male and 78 kg female. Each step up in seat numbers lowers the standard mass by 8 kg (1–5 to 6–9) and then 4 kg (6–9 to 10–19).

question: On an aeroplane with 10 to 19 passenger seats, what are the standard male and female masses?

options.text: Male 92 kg, female 74 kg
Male 92 kg, female 78 kg
Male 88 kg, female 70 kg
Male 96 kg, female 78 kg

explanation: For 10–19 seats the values are 92 kg male and 74 kg female, 4 kg above the 20-seat-plus values of 88 and 70 kg.

question: On an aeroplane with 19 seats or less, no hand baggage is carried in the cabin. What reduction may be made to the male and female standard masses?

options.text: 4 kg each
10 kg each
6 kg each
8 kg each

explanation: Where no hand baggage is carried in the cabin, or it is accounted for separately, 6 kg may be deducted from the male and female masses of the small aeroplane table. Children's masses are not reduced.

question: For the 6 kg hand baggage deduction, which item still does NOT count as hand baggage?

options.text: A laptop bag stowed overhead
A carry-on suitcase
A cabin trolley bag
An overcoat

explanation: Small items such as an overcoat, an umbrella, a small handbag, reading material or a small camera are not hand baggage, so the deduction is still allowed when only these are carried.

question: A flight is planned on a 12-seat aeroplane with 7 men, 3 women and 2 children, with hand baggage in the cabin. What standard passenger mass applies?

options.text: 976 kg
936 kg
876 kg
896 kg

explanation: The 10–19 seat values are 92 kg male, 74 kg female and 35 kg child: 7 × 92 + 3 × 74 + 2 × 35 = 644 + 222 + 70 = 936 kg. Deducting 6 kg per adult (876 kg) is wrong because hand baggage is carried; 896 kg and 976 kg come from the 20-seat and 6–9 seat rows.

question: On an aeroplane with 19 passenger seats or less, how is the mass of checked baggage determined?

options.text: By the 11 kg domestic standard per piece
By the 13 kg standard per piece
By a verbal statement from each passenger
By weighing it

explanation: Standard baggage masses apply only from 20 passenger seats upward. With 19 seats or less, the actual mass of checked baggage, found by weighing, must be used.

question: What is the standard mass per piece of checked baggage on a domestic flight (20 or more seats)?

options.text: 10 kg
13 kg
11 kg
15 kg

explanation: Domestic flights use 11 kg per piece, flights within the European region 13 kg, intercontinental flights 15 kg, and all other flights 13 kg.

question: What is the standard mass per piece of checked baggage on an intercontinental flight?

options.text: 17 kg
15 kg
11 kg
13 kg

explanation: Intercontinental flights, with origin and destination on different continents, use 15 kg per piece. Longer journeys tend to mean heavier bags.

question: What standard mass per piece of checked baggage is used on a flight within the European region, and on "all other" flights?

options.text: 13 kg for both
11 kg and 13 kg
15 kg for both
13 kg and 15 kg

explanation: Flights within the European region and all other flights not covered elsewhere both use 13 kg per piece. Only domestic (11 kg) and intercontinental (15 kg) differ.

question: For the baggage tables, what is a domestic flight?

options.text: A flight within the European region
A flight that begins and ends within one State
A flight between two airports of the same operator
A flight of less than one hour block time

explanation: A domestic flight has its origin and destination within the borders of one State. A flight between two States in Europe is a European-region flight instead.

question: For the baggage tables, what is an intercontinental flight?

options.text: Any flight that leaves the European region at any point
Any flight that needs an oceanic clearance
One between two different continents
Any flight longer than 3 000 NM

explanation: An intercontinental flight, other than a flight within the European region, has its origin and destination in different continents. Distance alone does not decide it.

question: Roughly which area defines "flights within the European region" for baggage masses?

options.text: Between about 27°N and 72°N, from 30°W to 45°E
The member States of the European Union only
Between 35°N and 70°N, from 10°W to 30°E
Everywhere north of the equator, from 30°W to 60°E

explanation: The European region is bounded by rhumb lines joining points that reach from 72°N down to 27°N and from 30°W to 45°E, so it includes North Africa, the Canary Islands and parts of the Middle East.

question: An operator wants to use standard masses other than the tabulated ones. What must it do first?

options.text: Use them on routes where the tables seem too high
Apply them for one season, then report the results
Notify passengers on their tickets
Get prior approval for a weighing survey plan

explanation: The operator must give its reasons to the authority and obtain approval in advance, submitting a detailed weighing survey plan and using the prescribed statistical method. Only after the results are verified and approved may the revised values be used.

question: Who may use revised standard masses obtained from an approved weighing survey?

options.text: Any operator on the same routes
Every operator in the same State
Only the operator that carried out the survey
Every operator flying the same aeroplane type

explanation: Revised standard masses apply only to the operator that ran the survey, and only in circumstances consistent with those under which the survey was done.

question: An approved survey gives a value higher than the standard tables. Which value must be used?

options.text: The tabulated standard value
Whichever value the commander prefers
The average of the two values
The higher survey value

explanation: Where revised standard masses exceed those in the tables, the higher values must be used. A survey can never be used to justify lighter masses than reality.

question: A flight carries a significant number of passengers expected to be heavier than the standard mass (for example a sports team). What must the operator do?

options.text: Weigh them or add an adequate mass increment
Reduce their checked baggage allowance to compensate
Use the all-adult mass instead of male and female masses
Use the standard masses, since they are averages

explanation: When many passengers are expected to exceed the standard mass, their actual mass must be found by weighing or by adding an adequate increment. The same applies to a significant amount of baggage heavier than the standard.

question: Many passengers check in baggage expected to exceed the standard baggage mass. What must be done?

options.text: Load it in the aft hold to keep the CG within limits
Weigh it or add an adequate mass increment
Nothing; standard baggage values are averages
Use the intercontinental 15 kg value

explanation: If standard baggage values are used but a significant number of bags are expected to be heavier, the operator must find their actual mass by weighing or add an adequate increment.

question: A non-standard method has been used to find the mass of the load. What must happen?

options.text: The flight must be delayed until all passengers are weighed
The load sheet is signed by the authority before departure
The commander is told and the method is stated in the documentation
The commander must add a 5% margin to the take-off mass

explanation: The commander must be advised whenever a non-standard method was used for the load, and the method must be stated in the mass and balance documentation.

question: When must mass and balance documentation be established?

options.text: Once per day for each aeroplane
Before each flight
Only when the take-off mass is close to the maximum
Only for flights carrying cargo

explanation: Documentation specifying the load and its distribution must be prepared before every flight, so the commander can confirm that the mass and balance limits are not exceeded.

question: Who must confirm by signature that the load and its distribution agree with the mass and balance documentation?

options.text: The commander only
The person who prepared the documentation
The operator's nominated post holder
The person supervising the loading

explanation: The person supervising loading signs to confirm the load matches the documentation. The person who prepared it must be named on it, and the commander shows acceptance by countersignature or equivalent.

question: How does the commander show acceptance of the mass and balance documentation?

options.text: By countersignature or equivalent
By an entry in the technical log
By a radio call to the handling agent
No acceptance is needed if the load is within limits

explanation: The document must be acceptable to the commander, who indicates acceptance by countersignature or an equivalent means such as an electronic acknowledgement.

question: Which item is required in the mass and balance documentation?

options.text: The route of the flight
The planned cruise level
The passengers' names
The trip fuel mass

explanation: Required items include registration and type, flight number and date, commander, preparer, DOM and its CG, take-off fuel and trip fuel, consumables, load components, take-off, landing and zero fuel masses, load distribution, CG positions and limiting values.

question: Which mass values must the mass and balance documentation show?

options.text: Take-off and ramp mass only
Take-off, landing and zero fuel mass
Maximum structural masses only
Landing mass and basic empty mass only

explanation: The documentation must give the take-off mass, landing mass and zero fuel mass, together with the limiting mass and CG values they are checked against.

question: Which person's identity must appear in the mass and balance documentation?

options.text: The commander's
The refuelling operator's
The dispatcher who planned the route
The senior cabin crew member's

explanation: The documentation must identify the commander and the person who prepared it, along with the aeroplane and flight details.

question: Under what condition may some required data be left out of the mass and balance documentation?

options.text: If the aeroplane is well below its maximum masses
If the commander agrees verbally
With the approval of the authority
If the flight is shorter than one hour

explanation: An operator may omit some of the data, but only with the approval of the authority.

question: After the documentation is complete, a last minute change occurs. What is required?

options.text: Tell the loading supervisor only
Inform the commander and enter it on the documentation
Cancel the documentation and start again in every case
Nothing if the change is less than 500 kg

explanation: Any last minute change must be brought to the commander's attention and entered on the documentation. New documentation is needed only if the change exceeds the limit set in the Operations Manual.

question: Where is the maximum last minute change in passengers or hold load specified, and what happens if it is exceeded?

options.text: In the flight manual; the commander decides
On the load sheet; the excess is offloaded
In the technical log; the CG is rechecked only
Operations Manual; new documentation is made

explanation: The maximum allowed last minute change is in the Operations Manual. If it is exceeded, new mass and balance documentation must be prepared.

question: How often must the output of a computerised mass and balance system be verified?

options.text: At intervals not exceeding 6 months
Only when the software changes
At intervals not exceeding 12 months
Before every flight

explanation: The operator must check that amendments to input data are incorporated and that the system works correctly, verifying the output at intervals not exceeding 6 months.

question: What is needed to use an onboard mass and balance computer system as the primary source for despatch?

options.text: Nothing beyond normal maintenance
Agreement of the manufacturer only
Approval by the authority
A second, identical system on board

explanation: An operator must obtain the authority's approval to use an onboard mass and balance system as the primary source for despatch.

question: Mass and balance documentation is sent to the aeroplane by datalink. What must remain available on the ground?

options.text: The draft before last minute changes
The final accepted documentation
Only the zero fuel mass and CG
Nothing; the aeroplane holds the record

explanation: When documentation is sent by datalink, a copy of the final version as accepted by the commander must be available on the ground.

question: When may a new aeroplane enter service without being reweighed by the operator?

options.text: Never; every operator must weigh before first use
When it is within 2% of the fleet mean mass
Only after its first scheduled maintenance check
If factory-weighed and records cover any modifications

explanation: New aeroplanes are normally weighed at the factory and may enter service without reweighing if the mass and balance records have been adjusted for any alterations or modifications.

question: An aeroplane moves between two operators with approved mass control programmes. When must the receiving operator weigh it before use?

options.text: If over four years since its last weighing
Never, if the previous records are complete
When more than two years have passed since its last weighing
Always, before its first flight

explanation: The receiving operator need not weigh it unless more than four years have elapsed since the last weighing.

question: An aeroplane is operated with individual mass values. What is the standard maximum interval between weighings?

options.text: Nine years
48 months for each fleet
Four years
Two years

explanation: Individual aeroplanes are reweighed at least every four years when individual masses are used; when fleet masses are used the interval is nine years. The interval itself is defined by the operator within these limits.

question: Between weighings, when must an aeroplane's mass and CG be re-established by weighing or by justified calculation?

options.text: When any single item over 10 kg is added
When the CG moves by more than 1% MAC
When DOM changes total over ±0.5% of maximum landing mass
When cumulative DOM changes exceed ±1% of the maximum take-off mass

explanation: Re-establishment is needed whenever cumulative changes to the DOM exceed ±0.5% of the maximum landing mass, or the cumulative CG change exceeds 0.5% of the MAC.

question: What cumulative change in CG position requires the aeroplane's mass and CG to be re-established?

options.text: More than 0.5 inch from the datum
More than 0.5% of the mean aerodynamic chord
More than 2% of the mean aerodynamic chord
More than 1% of the mean aerodynamic chord length

explanation: A cumulative CG change of more than 0.5% MAC, like a DOM change of more than ±0.5% of the maximum landing mass, triggers a new weighing or a justified calculation.

question: Who must carry out the weighing of an aeroplane?

options.text: The manufacturer or an approved maintenance organisation
Any calibrated weighbridge operator at the airport
The commander before each flight
The operator's flight operations department

explanation: Weighing must be done by the manufacturer or an approved maintenance organisation, with calibrated equipment.

question: Which precaution is part of the normal weighing procedure?

options.text: Weighing with the crew on board
Weighing outdoors on a level apron
Weighing with full fuel tanks and all oils
Weighing inside an enclosed building

explanation: Normal precautions include checking the aeroplane and equipment are complete, accounting for fluids, ensuring the aeroplane is clean, and weighing in an enclosed building to avoid wind effects.

question: Within what period must weighing scales be calibrated?

options.text: One year, or the maker's longer period
Four years, at the same time as the aeroplane
Two years, or the maker's shorter period
Five years, unless a fault is found

explanation: Each scale must be calibrated within two years or within the period the equipment manufacturer defines, whichever is less, by the manufacturer, a civil department of weights and measures or an authorised organisation.

question: When may a fleet of aeroplanes use an average dry operating mass and CG?

options.text: When they are the same type, whatever the configuration
When the operator has more than ten of them
When each aeroplane has been weighed in the last year
Same model and configuration, within tolerances

explanation: A fleet of the same model and configuration may use an average DOM and CG, provided each aeroplane's values meet the fleet tolerances.

question: An aeroplane's DOM differs from the fleet DOM by more than what amount, so that it must leave the fleet?

options.text: ±0.5% of the zero fuel mass
±0.5% of the maximum structural landing mass
±1% of the dry operating mass
±0.5% of the maximum take-off mass

explanation: An aeroplane whose DOM varies by more than ±0.5% of the maximum structural landing mass from the fleet DOM, or whose CG varies by more than ±0.5% MAC, is omitted from that fleet.

question: An aeroplane is within the fleet mass tolerance but its CG is outside the fleet CG tolerance. How may it be operated?

options.text: With the fleet mass but its individual CG
It must be removed from service
With the fleet mass and fleet CG plus a margin
With its individual mass and the fleet CG

explanation: If the mass is within tolerance but the CG is not, the aeroplane may still use the fleet dry operating mass with its own individual CG position.

question: One aeroplane has a different galley that takes it outside the fleet tolerance. How can it stay in the fleet?

options.text: It cannot; it must form a fleet of its own
By applying corrections to its mass and/or CG
By adding ballast until it matches the fleet mean
By reweighing it every month

explanation: A physical, accurately accountable difference such as galley or seat layout allows the aeroplane to stay in the fleet if appropriate corrections are applied to its mass and/or CG.

question: How must aeroplanes with no published mean aerodynamic chord be operated?

options.text: With fleet values and a 2% mass margin
With the CG assumed at the datum
With fleet values based on the nearest similar type
Individual values, or a special study

explanation: Without a published MAC, the fleet CG tolerance cannot be applied, so these aeroplanes use individual mass and CG values or are subject to a special study and approval.

question: An aeroplane in a fleet has not been weighed since the last fleet evaluation. When may it stay in the fleet?

options.text: Only if it is weighed before its next flight
Always, until the next fleet evaluation
If recomputed values stay within tolerance
Only if it has had no modifications at all

explanation: Such an aeroplane may stay in the fleet if its individual values, revised by computation, remain within the tolerances. Otherwise the operator sets new fleet values or uses individual values.

question: How is a new aeroplane added to a fleet that uses fleet values?

options.text: Weighing or computation shows it is within tolerance
It is accepted if it is the same model as the fleet
It flies with individual values for its first year
It is weighed and the fleet mean is recalculated to include it

explanation: To add an aeroplane to a fleet using fleet values, the operator must verify by weighing or computation that its actual values lie within the tolerances.

question: A fleet has 3 aeroplanes using fleet values. How many must be weighed between two fleet mass evaluations?

options.text: All 3
None, if all were weighed at delivery

explanation: For fleets of 2 or 3 aeroplanes the minimum number of weighings is n, so all of them must be weighed.

question: A fleet has 7 aeroplanes using fleet values. What is the minimum number of weighings between fleet mass evaluations?
explanation: For 4 to 9 aeroplanes the minimum is (n + 3) ÷ 2 = (7 + 3) ÷ 2 = 5. Using (n + 51) ÷ 10 is the formula for fleets of 10 or more.

question: A fleet has 29 aeroplanes using fleet values. What is the minimum number of weighings between fleet mass evaluations?
explanation: For 10 or more aeroplanes the minimum is (n + 51) ÷ 10 = (29 + 51) ÷ 10 = 8. The (n + 3) ÷ 2 formula, giving 16, is only for fleets of 4 to 9.

question: Which aeroplanes of a fleet should be chosen for weighing?

options.text: Those with the most recent modifications
Those with the highest flight hours
Those not weighed for the longest time
Any chosen at random by the authority

explanation: When choosing which aeroplanes to weigh, those which have not been weighed for the longest time should be selected.

question: What is the maximum interval between two fleet mass evaluations?

options.text: 9 years
6 months
24 months
48 months

explanation: The interval between two fleet mass evaluations must not exceed 48 months, and the fleet values must be updated at least at the end of each evaluation.

question: Besides passengers and baggage, for which load items may an operator submit standard masses for approval?

options.text: The flight crew only
Fuel, instead of using its density
Other items of the traffic load
None; only passengers and baggage have standard masses

explanation: An operator may submit standard masses for other load items for approval, in addition to those for passengers and checked baggage.

question: Under whose supervision must aeroplane loading be carried out?

options.text: Qualified personnel
Any member of the cabin crew
The aerodrome authority
The commander in person

explanation: The operator must ensure loading is supervised by qualified personnel and that the freight loaded agrees with the data used for the mass and balance calculation.

question: Which is an additional structural limit that loading must respect?

options.text: Maximum crosswind for loading
Maximum load per running metre
Minimum cargo hold temperature on the ground
Maximum fuel temperature

explanation: Loading must respect floor strength limits, the maximum load per running metre, the maximum mass per cargo compartment and the maximum seating limits.

question: When must operational margins be applied to the certificated CG envelope?

options.text: Only on flights with more than 100 passengers
Unless the load distribution is accounted for exactly
Never; the certificated envelope is always used
Only when the aeroplane is at maximum take-off mass

explanation: Unless seat allocation is applied and the effects of passengers per row, cargo per compartment and fuel per tank are exactly accounted for, operational margins must be applied, considering possible deviations from the assumed distribution.

question: With free seating, what must the operator provide for?

options.text: Loading all baggage in the forward hold to balance them
Assigning every passenger a seat at the gate
Correction if passengers sit at a cabin extreme
Adding 5 kg per passenger to the standard mass

explanation: If free seating is used, procedures must ensure flight or cabin crew take corrective action if passengers choose seats at an extreme of the cabin length.

question: What must the in-flight CG procedures account for?

options.text: People moving and fuel use or transfer
Changes in outside air temperature during the climb
Only the fuel burned between take-off and landing
Only movement of the cabin trolleys

explanation: The operator must show its procedures fully account for the extreme variation in CG travel in flight caused by passenger and crew movement and fuel consumption or transfer.

question: In a weighing survey, how many passengers must be weighed at least on an aeroplane with 40 or more seats?

options.text: 500 passengers
1 000 passengers
The greater of the statistical sample and 50 per seat
The greater of the statistical sample and 2 000 passengers

explanation: The sample must be at least the greater of the statistically calculated number and, for 40 or more seats, 2 000 passengers. With fewer than 40 seats it is 50 × the seating capacity.

question: A weighing survey covers an aeroplane with 30 passenger seats. What is the fixed minimum sample size?

options.text: 600 passengers
2 000 passengers
1 500 passengers
3 000 passengers

explanation: Below 40 seats the minimum is 50 × seating capacity = 50 × 30 = 1 500 passengers, unless the statistical calculation gives a larger number.

question: What relative confidence range is used for the all-adult mass in a weighing survey?
explanation: The pilot sample uses a relative confidence range (accuracy) of 1% for all-adult averages and 2% for separate male and female averages. Baggage also uses 1%.

question: In a passenger weighing survey, how are infants weighed?

options.text: Not at all; a fixed 10 kg is added
Separately, as children
Separately, then halved
With the accompanying adult

explanation: Infants are weighed together with the accompanying adult, matching how standard masses include an infant on an adult's seat.

question: What is the minimum capacity of a passenger weighing machine in a survey?

options.text: 200 kg
150 kg
250 kg
120 kg

explanation: The machine must have a capacity of at least 150 kg, display in graduations of 500 g at most, and be accurate to within 0.5% or 200 g, whichever is greater.

question: What accuracy must a passenger weighing machine used in a survey have?

options.text: 0.5% or 200 g, whichever is greater
0.5% or 200 g, whichever is less
2% at all masses
1% or 500 g, whichever is the smaller

explanation: The machine must be accurate within 0.5% or 200 g, whichever is greater, with display graduations of no more than 500 g.

question: What is the minimum number of checked bags in a baggage weighing survey?

options.text: 50 per seat

explanation: The baggage procedure mirrors the passenger one with a 1% accuracy, and a minimum of 2 000 pieces of checked baggage must be weighed.

question: On an aeroplane with 6–9 seats, what increment is added to the surveyed average passenger mass to give the revised standard?

options.text: 4 kg
16 kg
6 kg
8 kg

explanation: For smaller aeroplanes increments are added: 16 kg for 1–5 seats, 8 kg for 6–9 seats and 4 kg for 10–19 seats. From 20 seats the averages are used directly.

question: On an aeroplane with 1–5 seats, what increment is added to the surveyed average passenger mass?

options.text: 4 kg
16 kg
8 kg
12 kg

explanation: The smallest aeroplanes get the largest increment, 16 kg, because a single heavy passenger has a greater effect on their mass and balance.

question: At what interval must a deviation from the revised standard masses be reviewed?

options.text: Not exceeding nine years
Not exceeding five years
Every fleet mass evaluation
Not exceeding two years

explanation: An approved deviation, found by the survey procedure, must be reviewed at intervals not exceeding five years.

question: On what male/female ratio are revised all-adult masses based for normal flights?
explanation: All-adult revised values assume 80% male and 20% female on all flights except holiday charters, which use 50/50.

question: To use a different male/female ratio on certain routes, what must the data show?

options.text: It covers at least 95% of actual ratios on 200 or more flights
It has been used by another operator for a year
It covers at least 84% of actual ratios on 100 or more flights
It matches the average ratio on at least 50 flights

explanation: The operator must show the alternative ratio is conservative and covers at least 84% of actual ratios on a sample of at least 100 representative flights.

question: How are surveyed average masses rounded?

options.text: Both are rounded up to the next whole kg
Passengers to the nearest 5 kg; baggage to the nearest kg
Both to the nearest 0.5 kg
Passengers to 1 kg; baggage to 0.5 kg

explanation: Average passenger masses are rounded to the nearest whole kilogram and checked baggage values to the nearest 0.5 kg.

question: Where may an item carried in the cabin be stowed?

options.text: Anywhere not blocking the aisle
Under any seat
Against any bulkhead
Only where it can be restrained

explanation: Each item carried in the cabin may be stowed only in a location capable of restraining it, and placarded mass limits must not be exceeded.

question: When may underseat stowage be used for cabin baggage?

options.text: Only during the cruise
Always, for items under 10 kg
If the seat has a restraint bar that holds it
Only for the seats in emergency exit rows

explanation: Underseat stowage may be used only if the seat is fitted with a restraint bar and the baggage is small enough to be adequately restrained by it.

question: When may items be stowed against a cabin bulkhead?

options.text: When each item is lighter than 5 kg and is secured
If it can restrain them and has a mass placard
Never, in any circumstances
When a cabin crew member sits next to it

explanation: Items must not be stowed in toilets or against bulkheads unless the bulkhead can restrain them against forward, sideways or upward movement and carries a placard with the greatest mass allowed.

question: When must checks of cabin baggage stowage be made?

options.text: Before take-off and landing, and when belt signs are on
Before the first flight of the day only
When requested by passengers
Only before take-off

explanation: Checks must be made before take-off, before landing and whenever the fasten seat belt signs are on, so that baggage cannot block evacuation or fall and injure someone.

question: Which stowage rule concerns emergency equipment?

options.text: Baggage may cover it if the cabin crew know where it is
Baggage must not impede access to it
Emergency equipment must be stowed in the overhead lockers
Baggage must be at least 2 m from it

explanation: Baggage and cargo must not be placed where they can impede access to emergency equipment, and items in lockers must not stop latched doors from closing.
